bill.title: A joint resolution proposing a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution of the United States.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution proposes a constitutional amendment that requires federal expenditures and receipts to be balanced, which may occur over more than one year. Under the amendment, expenditures include all federal expenditures except those for payment of debt. Receipts do not include receipts derived from borrowing. The amendment requires Congress to achieve balance within 10 years of the ratification of the amendment. In an emergency situation, Congress may authorize additional expenditures that are not otherwise permitted by the amendment if two-thirds of the House of Representatives and the Senate agree to pass the bill. The additional expenditures must be for a limited time, and debts incurred from the expenditures must be paid as soon as practicable.

classification.plainSummary: This joint resolution proposes a constitutional amendment requiring the federal government to balance its spending and revenue, either in a single year or averaged over multiple years. Congress would have ten years after ratification to achieve balance. In emergencies, two-thirds of both the House and Senate could authorize additional spending for a limited time, with debts repaid as soon as practicable.

plain.whatItDoes: This joint resolution would propose a constitutional amendment that requires federal expenditures and receipts to be balanced, which may occur over more than one year.
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who pays tax or gets a federal payment.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in federal spending and borrowing. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
